title: The New Perspective on Paul
lead: The New Perspective is a way of reading Paul that began with E. P. Sanders's book Paul and Palestinian Judaism (1977). Sanders argued that Judaism of Paul's day was not a religion of earning salvation but of 'covenantal nomism': one gets in by God's grace in the covenant and stays in by keeping the law. James Dunn and N. T. Wright built on this, reading Paul's argument about 'works of the law' as concerned with who belongs to God's people. The related 'Paul within Judaism' reading (Nanos, Gager, Eisenbaum, Fredriksen) holds that Paul never left Judaism and wrote to Gentiles.

sections.h: What changed and what did not
sections.b: Older Protestant readings heard Paul rejecting Jewish legalism. The New Perspective hears him dealing with Jews and Gentiles in one family. Critics (Carson, Gathercole, Schreiner, Moo, Westerholm) say Sanders's picture of Judaism is too rosy, and that Paul does speak of human inability to keep the law. Many scholars now speak of 'perspectives' (Old, New, Apocalyptic, Radical) and hold parts of each.
